new_statements.quote: Najamba is a tonal language. H is high tone, L is low tone. Syllables may be H, L, falling <HL>, rising <LH>, or bell-shaped <LHL>. All regular stems (nouns, verbs, adjectives, numerals) have a lexical tone melody with one (rarely two) H-tone element(s). Some stems have /H/ lexical tone melody, others have /LH/, /HL/, or /LHL/ melody, spread out over the relevant number of syllables, but none is lexically all-L toned. [p. 9] ... Najamba shows relatively little of the metrical patterning that pervades the phonology (especially the verb morphophonology) of the northern Dogon languages that I have studied [...] However, "stem-final" is not a metrically defined position in the usual sense. [p. 17]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Najamba is a tone language with lexical tone melodies (/H/, /LH/, /HL/, /LHL/) on all stems and grammatical tone overlays; the grammar contains no statement of word stress at all, and its only metrical remark is that Najamba shows little metrical (syllable-reduction) patterning and that stem-final is not a metrically defined position.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Heath notes the light/heavy stem distinction is 'less important in Najamba than in some other Dogon languages' (§3.1.3, p. 17) and is a matter of tone-overlay mapping rather than weight.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/stem level lexical tone; tone overlays operate at word and phrase (tonosyntactic) level. No citation-form stress discussed. Hantgan et al. 2024 (Kindige variety) speculate in passing about iambic feet and a 'prominence clash' but make no stress claim.
new_statements.identity_note: Heath's grammar describes Najamba proper (villages Kubewel and Adia, in the valleys west of Douentza) and states (p. 2) that it 'does not describe Kindigué or Bondu varieties'; Najamba-Kindigué-Bondu is the whole dialect complex that Glottolog Hantgan & Davis 2012, Green & Hantgan 2019 and Hantgan et al. 2024 describe the Kindige (Koira/Kolobinye) variety, which Heath treats as a dialect of the same language; Glottolog has no separate code for Kindige that I saw. The plateau 'Bondu' varieties (Borko, Dogani, Tintam) remain undescribed except for Kassambara 1987.

sources.locator: §2.1 Prosody, p. 9; and §3.1.2 Embryonic metrical structure, p. 17
sources.note: No word-stress statement anywhere. §2.1 Prosody (p. 9): 'Najamba is a tonal language' with H/L/HL/LH/LHL syllable tones and lexical melodies /H/, /LH/, /HL/, /LHL/, overridden by grammatical tone overlays. §3.1.2 'Embryonic metrical structure' (p. 17): Najamba shows little of the metrical patterning of northern Dogon; 'stem-final is not a metrically defined position'. §3.1.3 (p. 17): light/heavy stem distinction 'less important in Najamba'. The word 'stress' occurs only in an etymological aside ('originated as an unstressed there'); 'accent' only as a tone-mark term.

sources.note: No stress statement. Concentrates on the Kindige variety (one male speaker, Douentza, 2008-2010). Speculates that an epenthetic vowel may avoid 'a problematic prominence clash' and that the Perfective stem 'presumably yields... an unbalanced (CV.CVV) iamb', calling for 'a closer study of metrification across the language'.
